subject: Critical Thinking
title: Premises and Conclusions: The Building Blocks
description: A micro-lesson that makes Premises and Conclusions: The Building Blocks usable.

hook.text: 'All humans are mortal. Socrates is human. Therefore, Socrates is mortal.' Three sentences. Two premises.

buildup.text: Premises are the evidence or reasons. The conclusion is what they support.

twist.text: Many arguments bury their weakest premise. Making all premises explicit is how you find the flaw.

climax.text: Challenge: take any argument you encounter today. Identify the conclusion. List every premise. Find the hidden one.

punchline.text: Every argument has a hidden premise. Finding it is half the battle.

quiz.question: What is a 'hidden premise' in an argument?
options: An unstated assumption required for the argument to work

details.summary: Every argument contains premises (the supporting evidence) and a conclusion (the claim being defended). Learning to identify each lets you see whether the reasoning actually holds together.
details.whyItMatters: Without recognizing premises and conclusions, you cannot tell if someone's reasoning supports their claim or merely asserts it.
takeaways: Premises are the reasons offered in support of a conclusion
Indicator words like 'because' and 'therefore' flag structure
Hidden premises often do the most argumentative work

faq.question: How can you identify the conclusion of an argument?
faq.answer: Look for indicator words like 'therefore,' 'hence,' or 'so.' The conclusion is the main claim the speaker wants you to accept. Everything else supports it.

faq.question: What is a hidden or unstated premise in an argument?
faq.answer: A hidden premise is an assumption the argument relies on but never states explicitly. Surfacing these hidden assumptions is one of the most powerful moves in critical analysis.
